Today we introduce Maple-Preview, an open-source 20B-A1B ternary-weight reasoning LLM, SOTA in its weight class. Maple-Preview can solve IMO-level problems and runs at over 200 tokens/sec on an M4 Mac Mini, 5–16x faster than efficient models like Gemma 4, Qwen3.5, and gpt-oss. Maple-Preview's light footprint enables on-device adaptation, made possible by the model's speed, energy, and memory efficiency. In early experiments, Maple-Preview is able to learn on the fly while running locally on a MacBook Pro. It autonomously decides which facts and user preferences to remember and then "dreams" about them later to embed that knowledge into its weights. This approach helps the model retain subtle, user-specific details that text-based memories may miss and addresses the scalability challenges of growing context. We believe that in the future, edge models will learn preferences by adapting their weights rather than through thousands of facts scattered across .md files, embedding user preferences into their own truly personal agent. At DeepGrove, we study how efficient models learn, rethinking architecture, training infrastructure, optimization, and hardware design to treat low precision as a first-class citizen. Maple-Preview serves as the first step in our journey toward efficient and adaptable intelligence. 🍁 Try Maple-Preview: https://chat.deepgrove.ai 🤗 Weights: https://lnkd.in/g-rzybJk 🖥️ MLX format: https://lnkd.in/grQaNPu6 📖 Local setup guide: https://lnkd.in/gSKNw3QW ✍️ Blog: https://lnkd.in/gdE8Z9YD

I recently took up a temporary part-time retail sales role, and it gave me an unexpected reminder that user experience (UX) is not just about websites or apps. UX exists in the physical store, the product display, the staff onboarding process, the point-of-sale (POS) workflow, the stock system, the product catalogue, and the way customers are guided from “just browsing” to finding something meaningful. What stood out to me was the contrast between the in-store customer experience and the digital version. In-store, new customers often began with curiosity. They were first drawn in by the window display, then browsed curated displays, noticed colour groupings, and slowly discovered the collections through the narrative shared by the sales team. That journey felt natural: visual attraction first, then curiosity, then story, then product consideration. Online, many e-commerce websites do the reverse. They open like catalogues: product grids, categories, collection names, filters, prices. That may be efficient for returning customers, but for someone new to the brand, it can feel transactional, especially when the brand’s real strength lies in storytelling, craftsmanship, place, and emotional discovery. It made me ask: How might we make a website feel less like “shop all products” and more like “step into the store”? A stronger digital experience could mirror the physical journey: Starting with a visual window display, the customers browse through the "rooms"; ultimately the craft and brand story are brought into the discovery flow. At the same time, the role also made me think about the internal UX. As a newcomer with no retail sales training, I noticed much of the operational knowledge lived informally in people’s heads: product characteristics, selling points, pairing logic, stock quirks, bundle deals and “how things are usually done.” When onboarding depends mostly on verbal guidance and memory, mistakes become more likely — not because people are careless or less capable, but because the system has not made the right information visible at the right moment. This was especially clear at checkout, where bundle deals had to be remembered, checked for eligibility, and keyed in manually as custom POS discounts — all while keeping the customer experience smooth. That is also UX. Good design reduces guesswork. It supports new staff by making hidden knowledge visible. It helps people serve customers consistently without relying entirely on memory, assumptions, or whoever happens to be present that day. The biggest takeaway for me: customer experience and employee experience are deeply connected. A polished customer-facing journey is hard to sustain when the behind-the-scenes systems are unclear, undocumented, or unsupported. Design is not only what the customer sees. It is the system that helps people care, choose, serve, and connect.

Why I Said "No" to a Full-Time Offer to Say "Yes" to Self-Investment. I recently received a full-time job offer. On paper, it was a step up in structure and workflow compared to my most recent experience. Yet, the final compensation package landed about 8% below my expected anchor. In the past, the conventional corporate script would dictate standard negotiation tactics, or perhaps a compromise to secure the predictability of a monthly paycheck. Instead, I chose to bow out graciously. Stepping away made me realise a profound truth: We often focus so much on the market value companies place on us, that we forget to calculate the value we place on our own time. For 20 years, my prime was dedicated entirely to raising a beautiful family and managing caregiving responsibilities. Now that my home base is settled and those heavy seasons have naturally concluded, I find myself in a rare, vibrant window of life. By declining an offer that did not fully align, I did not lose an opportunity. I chose to keep complete control of my time—and invest it directly back into myself. What I have realised is that skills do not expire just because you step away from a corporate desk. The analytical training from my university years and the strategic navigation required during my working life did not vanish; they simply transferred. Lately, I have been applying that foundational problem solving toolkit to run my own personal "growth accelerator," driven by trial, error, and curiosity: Mental Fitness: To push through the steep curves of mastering Japanese while being mindful of budget and to re-visit conversational Korean to prepare for an upcoming trip. Creative Frictions: Using systematic trial-and-error to discover the precision and patience required for artisan bread making and flower arrangement. Physical Strength: Staying disciplined with structured fitness classes and heavy compound lifting at the gym. Up next on the horizon? Setting up violin lessons to introduce a completely new layer of creative challenge. True mental stimulation and critical thinking do not happen only within a 9-to-5 frame. They happen when you give your brain the freedom to adapt, fail, learn, and create using the lifetime of skills you've already built. If you are currently navigating a career transition or stepping into a new chapter of life, remember this: You are not "underemployed" if you are actively self-invested. Don't be afraid to own your time, leverage your foundational strengths, and build a life portfolio that actually fulfills you. #CareerTransitions #SelfInvestment #ContinuousLearning #PersonalGrowth #MidLifeRenaissance #WorkLifeDesign
